chapters.title: Chapter 2: Understanding the Asset Classes You're Trading

lessons.title: Equities and Equity Indices: Nifty 50, Bank Nifty, and Sectoral Indices as Systematic Instruments

body.text: An index is not just a number on a screen, it is a rules-based portfolio that someone else rebalances for you on a fixed schedule. Trading Nifty 50 futures means trading that rulebook, not fifty individual bets, and a systematic strategy needs to understand the rulebook as closely as it understands the price.

children.text: Equities are the most familiar asset class in this course, but familiarity hides real mechanical detail that matters once a strategy is systematic rather than discretionary. This lesson covers how Nifty 50, Bank Nifty, and sectoral indices are actually constructed, why trading the index differs from trading a basket of its constituents, and two data traps, index reconstitution effects and survivorship bias, that quietly wreck backtests built without knowing this mechanics.
How Nifty 50 Is Actually Built: Free-Float Market Cap Weighting

markDefs.definition: The portion of a company's total shares that is actually available for public trading, excluding promoter holdings, government stakes, and other strategic holders. Index weights are calculated on this smaller, tradable share count, not total shares outstanding.

children.text: NSE Indices Limited maintains Nifty 50 as a

-weighted index of the fifty largest, most liquid NSE-listed companies, with individual stock and sector weight caps applied to prevent any single name or sector from dominating the index. This means the index's day-to-day move is driven disproportionately by its largest, most liquid constituents, not equally by all fifty. A momentum or trend signal built on Nifty futures is, underneath the single ticker, mostly a bet on how a handful of large banking, IT, and energy names are behaving.

Sectoral Indices (Nifty IT, Auto, Pharma, FMCG, Metal, and similar)

children.text: Why Trade the Index, Not the Basket of Stocks

A systematic desk that wants exposure to broad Indian equity beta almost always trades Nifty 50 futures rather than buying all fifty constituents directly. One instrument means one bid-ask spread and one margin requirement instead of fifty, and Nifty and Bank Nifty futures are among the most liquid listed index derivatives anywhere, which keeps execution costs low relative to replicating the basket by hand. This matters more, not less, in a multi-asset system, since Chapter 8's backtesting work assumes transaction costs are realistic, and a fifty-leg replication strategy is a very different cost profile from a single futures contract.

children.text: Sectoral Indices: A Built-In Tool for Sector Rotation, With a Liquidity Catch

NSE publishes sectoral indices covering IT, auto, pharma, FMCG, metals, realty, and several other sectors, each a genuinely useful signal for a sector rotation strategy, since sectors rarely move in perfect lockstep with the broad index or each other. The catch is liquidity: Bank Nifty aside, most sectoral indices do not have deeply liquid exchange-traded futures or options. A systematic strategy that generates a signal on, say, Nifty Metal, often has to express that view through a basket of the underlying constituents, an ETF tracking the sector, or accept wider execution costs on a thinner derivatives contract if one exists at all. This is a real constraint on strategy design, not a detail to gloss over when backtests assume frictionless execution.

body.title: Free-Float Market Cap Weighting vs Equal Weighting

columns.label: Free-Float Market Cap Weighted (Nifty 50, Bank Nifty)
points: Largest, most liquid names dominate index moves
Naturally tilts toward whatever has already grown largest
Lower turnover at rebalancing, since weights adjust gradually with price
The standard benchmark most Indian systematic strategies are measured against

columns.label: Equal Weighted (Nifty50 Equal Weight)
points: Every constituent contributes the same weight regardless of size
More exposure to smaller constituents within the same 50 names
Higher turnover at rebalancing, since weights must be actively reset
Useful as a size-factor comparison against the standard index

children.text: Index Reconstitution: A Predictable Event a Systematic Trader Can Actually Model

Twice a year, NSE Indices reviews Nifty 50's constituents against its free-float market cap ranking and replaces names that have fallen out of the qualifying range with names that have grown into it, announced with an advance notice window before the change takes effect. Every fund that tracks the index has to buy the newly added stock and sell the removed one around the effective date, which creates measurable, somewhat anticipatable trading pressure, an effect well documented for index inclusions and exclusions in markets globally, not unique to India. This is not a strategy handed to you fully formed, but it is a genuinely useful, rules-based event a systematic desk can study and model, unlike most market moves, which are not announced in advance.

body.text: Most price-moving events are unpredictable by nature. Index reconstitution is one of the rare exceptions: the rule, the timing, and often the affected stocks are public information well before the trade has to happen. That combination of predictability and rules-based mechanics is exactly the kind of edge a systematic approach is built to exploit.

children.text: Corporate Actions and Survivorship Bias: The Data Trap

Stock splits, bonus issues, and dividends all require price adjustment before a backtest is meaningful, standard practice most data vendors handle automatically. The subtler trap is survivorship bias: building a backtest using today's Nifty 50 constituent list applied backward through history, as though those exact fifty names had always been the index. In reality, dozens of names have entered and exited Nifty 50 over the years as companies grew, shrank, merged, or were replaced at reconstitution. A backtest run on today's constituent list silently excludes every stock that was once in the index and later dropped out, typically because it performed badly, which biases the backtested results upward in a way that has nothing to do with the strategy's actual skill.

body.text: A backtest that only uses today's index members is quietly backtesting on survivors. Any stock's decline severe enough to get it dropped from the index is excluded from the very history meant to test how the strategy handles declines. This single mistake can turn a mediocre strategy into an apparently great one, purely on paper.

children.text: The fix is point-in-time constituent data: knowing exactly which fifty stocks were in Nifty 50 on any given historical date, not just today. This is more data-engineering effort than trading a single index future, but it is the difference between a backtest that means something and one that flatters itself.
What This Means for Signal Design in This Course

Most of the equity signals built later in this course trade Nifty 50 and Bank Nifty futures directly, precisely because their liquidity and single-instrument simplicity make execution assumptions realistic. Where a sectoral tilt genuinely improves a signal, this course is explicit about the liquidity trade-off involved in expressing it. The next lesson moves from equities to fixed income, an asset class with none of the free-float weighting mechanics covered here, and an entirely different, and in some ways simpler, set of instrument mechanics.

body.title: The Momentum Backtest That Looked Too Good
body.scenario: A quant researcher backtests a simple 12-month momentum strategy on "Nifty 50 stocks" from 2010 to 2024, using the current Nifty 50 constituent list applied across the entire period. The strategy shows an impressively smooth equity curve with very few large drawdowns, better than most published momentum results on Indian equities.
body.prompt: What is the most likely explanation for why this backtest looks unusually clean, and what would you check first?
body.modelAnswer: The most likely explanation is survivorship bias. By using today's Nifty 50 constituent list applied backward across fourteen years, the backtest silently excludes every stock that was in the index at some point but was later removed, typically because it underperformed badly enough to fall out of the free-float market cap ranking. Momentum strategies are directly exposed to this: some of a real momentum strategy's worst drawdowns come from holding a stock as its momentum reverses sharply, and if those exact stocks have been removed from the test universe because they later fell out of the index, the backtest never sees its own worst cases. The first thing to check is whether the researcher used point-in-time constituent data, the actual Nifty 50 membership as it stood on each historical date, rather than today's list projected backward.

body.title: Free-Float Weighting, Applied
body.question: Nifty 50 is free-float market cap weighted. What does this mean for how the index moves day to day?
options: All fifty constituents contribute equally to the index's daily move
The index only reflects government-held shares of each company
Larger, more liquid constituents drive a disproportionate share of the index's move, since weights are based on tradable float-adjusted market value
Weighting is fixed permanently at the index's original launch and never changes
body.explanation: Free-float market cap weighting means each constituent's index weight is proportional to its tradable share value, promoter and strategic holdings excluded. This means the largest, most liquid names have an outsized influence on the index's day-to-day move, unlike an equal-weighted index where every constituent counts the same.

body.title: Naming the Backtesting Trap
body.textWithBlank: Building a backtest using only an index's current constituent list, applied backward through history, silently excludes every stock that was once a member and later dropped out, a data problem known as ___.
body.explanation: Survivorship bias is one of the most common, and most quietly damaging, mistakes in systematic backtesting. It inflates backtested performance by removing exactly the poor performers a strategy needed to be tested against, without ever showing up as an obvious error in the code.

points: Nifty 50 is a free-float market cap weighted index maintained by NSE Indices Limited, with the largest and most liquid constituents driving a disproportionate share of its daily move
Trading the index future instead of a fifty-stock basket collapses execution cost and margin into a single, highly liquid instrument, which matters for realistic backtesting
Sectoral indices are useful signals for sector rotation, but most lack deep exchange-traded derivatives liquidity, unlike Nifty 50 and Bank Nifty
Index reconstitution happens on a known schedule and creates measurable, somewhat anticipatable trading pressure around the effective date, a rare predictable event in markets
Backtesting on today's index constituent list applied backward through history introduces survivorship bias, which inflates results by excluding stocks that were dropped for underperforming
Point-in-time constituent data, not the current index list, is required for a backtest to actually mean what it claims to mean
